pos: n. (the emmet; the sluggard's appointed teacher)
etymology: From Old English aemette, an emmet. The Hebrew is nemalah, used only in the two Proverbs passages — and in both the creature is set up as an instructor of men.
biblical_def: Proverbs sends a lazy man to school under an insect: “Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise” (Proverbs 6:6). The lesson is in what the ant does not have: “Which having no guide, overseer, or ruler” (Proverbs 6:7) — no foreman, no supervisor, no one checking — and yet, “Provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest” (Proverbs 6:8). The sluggard's defect is not ignorance of what needs doing; it is that he requires someone standing over him. The ant works to a season no one announces to her. Agur returns to the same creature among his four little things that are exceeding wise: “The ants are a people not strong, yet they prepare their meat in the summer” (Proverbs 30:25). Note the word people. Agur grants them a commonwealth and a polity, and their wisdom is entirely in timing — they do in summer what winter will require. Scripture's doctrine of work is here in miniature: labour is not a curse but a creation ordinance, given in the garden before the fall, and the curse fell on the ground and not on the working.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the ant as an emmet; a pismire — a small insect that lives in societies, and provides in summer for its winter sustenance.
webster_full: ANT, n. [Sax. aemet.] An emmet; a pismire. Ants constitute a genus of insects of the hymenopteral order.
ANT, n. These insects live in societies, forming nests or hillocks, and are remarkable for their industry.
EMMET, n. An ant or pismire; a small insect that lives in communities.
SLUGGARD, n. A person habitually lazy, idle and inactive; a drone.
PROVIDE, v.t. [L. provideo; pro and video, to see before.] To procure beforehand; to get, collect or make ready for future use; to prepare.
scriptures: Proverbs 6:6
Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise:
Proverbs 6:7
Which having no guide, overseer, or ruler,
Proverbs 6:8
Provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest.
Proverbs 30:25
The ants are a people not strong, yet they prepare their meat in the summer;
corruption_summary: Work is treated as a consequence of the fall to be minimized, or as an identity to be maximized, and Proverbs' plain creational account of diligence is lost between the two.
corruption_paragraphs: One error makes labour a curse. Genesis gives Adam the garden to dress and to keep before there is any sin in the world; the curse in Genesis 3 falls on the ground, adding thorns and sweat to work that was already good. A Christianity that treats employment as an unfortunate necessity between Sundays has a doctrine the first two chapters of the Bible contradict. The ant works because she was made to, and Proverbs finds her ways instructive rather than pitiable.

The opposite error makes labour the whole man. The same book that commends the ant commands the Sabbath, warns that it is vain to rise up early and sit up late eating the bread of sorrows, and tells the man who toils without an heir that this also is vanity. Proverbs 6:7 is worth a second look here: the ant has no overseer, and that is her commendation, not her tragedy. Diligence that requires a supervisor is not yet virtue; diligence that needs an audience has simply changed supervisors.
roots_summary: Hebrew nemalah (H5244), an ant; atsel (H6102), a sluggard; qayits (H7019), summer; qatsir (H7105), harvest.
roots_lines: Hebrew nemalah (H5244) — an ant; only Proverbs 6:6 and 30:25.
Hebrew atsel (H6102) — sluggard, slothful; a standing figure of Proverbs.
Hebrew qayits (H7019) — summer; the season of gathering against the winter.
Hebrew qatsin (H7101) — a chief, ruler; one of the three overseers the ant lacks.
Hebrew am (H5971) — a people; Agur's word for the ants, Proverbs 30:25.
usage: “Go to the ant, thou sluggard” — an insect set up as a teacher.
“Having no guide, overseer, or ruler” — and that is the commendation.
“A people not strong” — a commonwealth, wise in timing.

pos: n. (an unclean creeping thing; the plague-sign of the Philistines)
etymology: From Old English mus. The Hebrew akbar covers mouse, rat, and similar rodents. It appears in the law of clean and unclean, in Isaiah's indictment of secret cult meals, and in the strange episode of the golden mice sent back with the ark.
biblical_def: The mouse is named in the law among the creatures that defile: “These also shall be unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth; the weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise after his kind” (Leviticus 11:29). Isaiah then uses it to expose a cult whose adherents thought themselves holy: “They that sanctify themselves, and purify themselves in the gardens behind one tree in the midst, eating swine's flesh, and the abomination, and the mouse, shall be consumed together, saith the LORD” (Isaiah 66:17). The detail is devastating — these people are performing purification rituals while eating what God called unclean. Religion and rebellion in one act. The mouse appears again in Philistia, where the men of Ashdod, struck with a plague while the ark stood among them, send it home with a guilt offering: “Wherefore ye shall make images of your emerods, and images of your mice that mar the land; and ye shall give glory unto the God of Israel: peradventure he will lighten his hand from off you, and from off your gods, and from off your land” (1 Samuel 6:5). The law's general principle governs: “And every creeping thing that flieth is unclean unto you: they shall not be eaten” (Deuteronomy 14:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the mouse as a small animal of the genus Mus, inhabiting houses — the common domestic mouse.
webster_full: MOUSE, n. plu. mice. [Sax. mus.] A small animal of the genus Mus, inhabiting houses. The name is also applied to many other species of the genus.
MOUSE, v.i. To catch mice. To watch for and catch, as a cat.
UNCLEAN, a. Not clean; foul; dirty; filthy. In the Jewish law, ceremonially impure; not cleansed by ritual practices.
CREEPING, ppr. Moving on the belly, or with the body near the ground; moving slowly.
ABOMINATION, n. In Scripture, that which is exceedingly hateful and detestable to God; particularly, idols and idolatrous practices.
scriptures: Leviticus 11:29
These also shall be unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth; the weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise after his kind,
Isaiah 66:17
They that sanctify themselves, and purify themselves in the gardens behind one tree in the midst, eating swine's flesh, and the abomination, and the mouse, shall be consumed together, saith the LORD.
Deuteronomy 14:19
And every creeping thing that flieth is unclean unto you: they shall not be eaten.
Leviticus 11:20
All fowls that creep, going upon all four, shall be an abomination unto you.
corruption_summary: The dietary law is cited to prove that Scripture's moral commands are arbitrary and expired, which mistakes the ceremonial for the moral and ignores who abolished the one.
corruption_paragraphs: The argument is familiar: Leviticus forbids mice and shellfish, no one keeps that, therefore no one need keep what Leviticus says about anything else. Reformed theology has answered this for four centuries with a distinction the New Testament itself draws. The ceremonial law — food, festival, sacrifice, purification — was a shadow of good things to come and is fulfilled and abrogated in Christ; the moral law, summarized in the Ten Commandments, binds all men always. It was Christ who purged all meats, and Peter who was told not to call common what God had cleansed. The dietary code did not lapse by neglect; it was closed by the One it pointed to.

Isaiah 66:17 remains pointed for the church rather than against it. The people described are not pagans. They sanctify themselves, they purify themselves, and they are in a garden shrine eating mice. Scrupulous religious observance running alongside a forbidden practice is not a contradiction the human heart finds difficult; it is the normal condition of hypocrisy, and it is one of the few sins Christ attacked by name and at length.
roots_summary: Hebrew akbar (H5909), a mouse or rat; sherets (H8318), a swarming or creeping thing; tame (H2931), unclean; shiqquts (H8251), an abomination.

Hebrew sherets (H8318) — a swarming thing; the class the mouse belongs to.
Hebrew tame (H2931) — ceremonially unclean; the verdict of Leviticus 11.
Hebrew shiqquts (H8251) — a detestable thing; the abomination of Isaiah 66:17.
Greek koinos (G2839) — common, unclean; Acts 10:15, what God hath cleansed.
usage: “The weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise” — named in the law by kind.
“They that sanctify themselves…eating…the mouse” — ritual and rebellion in one act.
“Images of your mice that mar the land” — a pagan guilt offering.

pos: n. (the wild swine; what enters a vineyard whose hedge is down)
etymology: From Old English bar, a male swine. Psalm 80 uses the Hebrew chazir miyaar, the swine out of the wood — the wild boar, the most destructive animal a Mediterranean vine-grower could meet.
biblical_def: Psalm 80 is a lament over a vineyard, and the psalmist does not begin with the boar. He begins with the fence: “Why hast thou then broken down her hedges, so that all they which pass by the way do pluck her?” (Psalm 80:12). Only then does the animal appear: “The boar out of the wood doth waste it, and the wild beast of the field doth devour it” (Psalm 80:13). The order is the theology. Israel is not being destroyed because a boar happened by; the boar came because God removed the hedge, and the psalmist says so to God's face. A wild boar in a vineyard does not eat a crop so much as demolish the plantation — roots torn, vines uprooted, the work of years undone in a night. And the prayer that follows asks for the only remedy there is, which is not a stronger fence: “Return, we beseech thee, O God of hosts: look down from heaven, and behold, and visit this vine” (Psalm 80:14). The swine is an unclean beast by the law — among the creatures Israel could not eat, as Isaiah remembers when he indicts those “eating swine's flesh, and the abomination, and the mouse” (Isaiah 66:17) — so the picture is of the unclean loose in the LORD's own planting.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a boar as the male of swine not castrated; and a wild boar as the wild swine, a fierce animal of the forest.
webster_full: BOAR, n. [Sax. bar.] The male of swine not castrated.
BOARISH, a. Swinish; brutal; cruel.
SWINE, n. [Sax. swin.] A hog; a general name for that species of animal.
HEDGE, n. A thicket of thorn-bushes or other shrubs or small trees, planted to fence or inclose a field.
VINEYARD, n. A plantation of vines producing grapes; in Scripture, frequently a figure of the church or nation of Israel.
scriptures: Psalm 80:12
Why hast thou then broken down her hedges, so that all they which pass by the way do pluck her?
Psalm 80:13
The boar out of the wood doth waste it, and the wild beast of the field doth devour it.
Psalm 80:14
Return, we beseech thee, O God of hosts: look down from heaven, and behold, and visit this vine;
Isaiah 66:17
They that sanctify themselves, and purify themselves in the gardens behind one tree in the midst, eating swine's flesh, and the abomination, and the mouse, shall be consumed together, saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: Disaster is attributed to the boar — the visible enemy, the hostile culture — when the psalm puts the question about the hedge to God first.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 80 is a model of how a believing people reasons about calamity, and the church regularly reverses its order. The modern lament begins and ends with the boar: name the enemy, describe the damage, organize against it. The psalmist spends verse 12 asking God why the hedge is down, because he knows that no beast gets into a vineyard the Keeper is fencing. That question is not despair; it is faith taking the matter to the only Hand that could have opened the gap.

The doctrine underneath is the one Joseph stated to his brothers and Job to his wife: God's sovereignty extends over the boar. He is not the author of sin, and the boar is fully a boar and fully accountable for the wreckage. But the hedge is God's, the vine is God's, and the plea in verse 14 is directed accordingly — not drive out the beast but return, O God of hosts. A church that prays only against its enemies has skipped the two verses that would have made the prayer effectual.
roots_summary: Hebrew chazir (H2386), swine, boar; yaar (H3293), a wood, forest; gephen (H1612), a vine; gader (H1447), a wall or hedge.
roots_lines: Hebrew chazir (H2386) — swine; chazir miyaar, the boar out of the wood, Psalm 80:13.
Hebrew yaar (H3293) — a forest, wood; where the wild swine comes from.
Hebrew gader (H1447) — a fence, hedge; broken down in verse 12.
Hebrew gephen (H1612) — a vine; Israel as the LORD's planting, Isaiah 5:7.
Hebrew kirsem (H3765) — to lay waste, root up; the boar's particular ruin.
usage: “Why hast thou then broken down her hedges” — the first question, and it is to God.
“The boar out of the wood doth waste it” — the beast comes second.
“Return, we beseech thee” — not drive out the beast.

pos: n. (a leaping insect permitted for food in the law; probably a cricket or locust-kind)
etymology: From Old English bitela, a biter. The Hebrew chargol denotes a leaping insect; the KJV's beetle reflects seventeenth-century English usage for a broader class of insects than the modern word, since true beetles do not leap.
biblical_def: Among the flying creeping things, the law makes a narrow exception on a single anatomical test: “Yet these may ye eat of every flying creeping thing that goeth upon all four, which have legs above their feet, to leap withal upon the earth” (Leviticus 11:21). The criterion is jointed legs for leaping; everything else in the class is forbidden — “All fowls that creep, going upon all four, shall be an abomination unto you” (Leviticus 11:20). Four kinds pass: “Even these of them ye may eat; the locust after his kind, and the bald locust after his kind, and the beetle after his kind, and the grasshopper after his kind” (Leviticus 11:22). The exception matters historically, because it is what John the Baptist lived on in the wilderness. The general rule stands elsewhere plainly: “And every creeping thing that flieth is unclean unto you: they shall not be eaten” (Deuteronomy 14:19). The phrase repeated four times in verse 22 — after his kind — is the same formula as Genesis 1, and it carries the creational doctrine that God made fixed kinds and that the law reckons with the world as He made it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the beetle as a genus of insects, the Scarabaeus, of many species, having hard cases or sheaths for the wings.
webster_full: BEETLE, n. [Sax. bitela, from bitan, to bite.] A genus of insects, termed by Linne, Scarabaeus. The generic characters are, clavated antennae, fissile longitudinally.
BEETLE, n. A heavy mallet or wooden hammer, used to drive wedges, beat pavements, &c.
LOCUST, n. [L. locusta.] An insect of the genus Gryllus, of many species, remarkable for the devastation it makes.
GRASSHOPPER, n. An insect of the genus Gryllus, which lives among grass, and is remarkable for leaping.
KIND, n. Race; genus; generic class; sort, in a sense more loose than genus.
scriptures: Leviticus 11:21
Yet these may ye eat of every flying creeping thing that goeth upon all four, which have legs above their feet, to leap withal upon the earth;
Leviticus 11:22
Even these of them ye may eat; the locust after his kind, and the bald locust after his kind, and the beetle after his kind, and the grasshopper after his kind.
Leviticus 11:20
All fowls that creep, going upon all four, shall be an abomination unto you.
Deuteronomy 14:19
And every creeping thing that flieth is unclean unto you: they shall not be eaten.
corruption_summary: A translator's word-choice from 1611 is presented as a scientific error in Scripture, since beetles do not leap — which confuses the English rendering with the Hebrew text.
corruption_paragraphs: The objection is stated confidently and rests on a confusion. Leviticus 11:22 has chargol, a leaping insect, and the verse before it defines the permitted class by the presence of jointed legs for leaping — the Hebrew is internally exact. Beetle in seventeenth-century English covered a wider range of insects than it does now, and the translators used the everyday word of their day for an insect they could not identify more precisely. The dictionary's doctrine of inspiration is of the original autographs; a translation choice is the work of godly men and not itself inspired, which is why the objection, even if pressed, reaches nothing that Scripture claims.

After his kind, repeated four times in one verse, is the more substantial matter. The formula is Genesis 1's, and it is doing work here: the law sorts creation by the categories God established at creation rather than by categories Israel found convenient. The whole structure of clean and unclean teaches a nation to make distinctions because its God makes them. That habit — holy and common, clean and unclean, kind and kind — was the schoolmaster, and the New Testament sets aside the diet while keeping the discipline of discernment it trained.

Hebrew arbeh (H697) — the locust; the plague of Exodus 10 and the food of Matthew 3:4.
Hebrew chagab (H2284) — a grasshopper; Numbers 13:33, how the spies felt.
Hebrew min (H4327) — kind, species; the Genesis 1 formula repeated four times here.
Hebrew sheqets (H8263) — a detestable thing; the verdict on the rest of the class.
usage: “Legs above their feet, to leap withal” — the anatomical test.
“The beetle after his kind” — Genesis 1's formula inside the law.
“All fowls that creep…shall be an abomination” — the rule the exception cuts.

pos: n. pl. (a hen's young; the figure of Christ's lament over Jerusalem)
etymology: From Old English cicen, the young of the domestic fowl. Matthew 23:37 renders Greek nossia, a brood. The image is the commonest sight in a Judean yard, chosen for the most sorrowful sentence in the Gospels.
biblical_def: At the end of the woes on the scribes and Pharisees, the tone breaks entirely: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!” (Matthew 23:37). Luke records the same words with the collective noun: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent unto thee; how often would I have gathered thy children together, as a hen doth gather her brood under her wings, and ye would not!” (Luke 13:34). The figure is domestic and it is also lethal: a hen covering her chickens in a fire dies in the covering, and that is what the speaker was days away from doing. How often looks back across the whole history of a nation that stoned the men sent to it. And the last clause is the tragedy: ye would not. The prophets had said the same in their own idiom — a people mourning like doves and looking for a judgment that does not come: “We roar all like bears, and mourn sore like doves: we look for judgment, but there is none; for salvation, but it is far off from us” (Isaiah 59:11). Christ weeps over the city that kills Him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chicken as the young of fowls; a young hen or cock — and by extension, a person of tender years.
webster_full: CHICKEN, n. [Sax. cicen.] The young of fowls, particularly of the domestic hen, or gallinaceous fowls.
CHICKEN, n. A person of tender years.
HEN, n. [Sax. henne.] The female of the gallinaceous kind of fowls.
BROOD, n. Offspring; progeny; formerly used of human beings, but now of fowls and other oviparous animals.
GATHER, v.t. To bring together; to collect a number of separate things; to assemble.
scriptures: Matthew 23:37

O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!
Luke 13:34

O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent unto thee; how often would I have gathered thy children together, as a hen doth gather her brood under her wings, and ye would not!
Isaiah 59:11
We roar all like bears, and mourn sore like doves: we look for judgment, but there is none; for salvation, but it is far off from us.
Psalm 102:7
I watch, and am as a sparrow alone upon the house top.
corruption_summary: The verse is used to prove that God's saving will is finally defeated by the human will, when the sentence itself distinguishes the children Christ would have gathered from the city that would not let Him.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 23:37 is the standard text against effectual grace, and the grammar is worth reading slowly. Christ says He would have gathered thy children, and that ye would not — the pronouns are not the same people. The ye is the city addressed through the verse, the leadership that killed the prophets and stoned the messengers and kept the children from coming. The verse is an indictment of men who obstructed, not an admission that the Son of God attempted a gathering and failed. Christ's own words a chapter earlier have the Son revealing the Father to whomsoever He will.

The Reformed reading does not blunt the grief, and the grief is the point. Here is the tenderest image in Scripture — a hen with her chickens under her wing — in the mouth of the Judge pronouncing a city's desolation. The 1689 confesses both that God ordains whatsoever comes to pass and that He has no pleasure in the death of the wicked. A theology that cannot weep at Matthew 23:37 has not understood it, and neither has one that concludes from it that God is a spectator to His own decree.
roots_summary: Greek nossion (G3556), a chick; nossia (G3555), a brood; ornis (G3733), a hen; episunago (G1996), to gather together.
roots_lines: Greek nossion (G3556) — a chick; Matthew 23:37, rendered chickens.
Greek nossia (G3555) — a brood; Luke 13:34, the collective form.
Greek ornis (G3733) — a bird, a hen; the figure Christ takes for Himself.
Greek episunago (G1996) — to gather together; the verb of the gathering He willed.
Hebrew kanaph (H3671) — a wing; Ruth 2:12, under whose wings thou art come to trust.
usage: “As a hen gathereth her chickens” — the tenderest figure, in a sentence of judgment.
“How often would I have gathered” — a nation's whole history in two words.
“And ye would not” — and the pronoun is not the children.

pos: n. (the cry of sheep; the sound that convicted Saul)
etymology: From Old English blaetan, to bleat. In 1 Samuel 15 the noun is the hinge of the story: Saul reports a completed obedience, and the animals he kept back are audible in the background while he says it.
biblical_def: Saul greets the prophet with a claim: he has performed the commandment of the LORD. Samuel answers with a question about noise: “And Samuel said, What meaneth then this bleating of the sheep in mine ears, and the lowing of the oxen which I hear?” (1 Samuel 15:14). The evidence against the report is simply audible; the spared flocks are announcing themselves. Saul's defence is that the animals were kept to sacrifice to the LORD, which makes the disobedience religious, and Samuel's reply is one of the great sentences of Scripture: “And Samuel said, Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams” (1 Samuel 15:22). Then the verdict: “For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Because thou hast rejected the word of the LORD, he hath also rejected thee from being king” (1 Samuel 15:23). The same sound appears in Deborah's song as the mark of men who stayed home from the LORD's war: “Why abodest thou among the sheepfolds, to hear the bleatings of the flocks? For the divisions of Reuben there were great searchings of heart” (Judges 5:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bleating as the cry of a sheep; and the verb, to make the noise of a sheep.
webster_full: BLEATING, ppr. Crying as a sheep.
BLEATING, n. The cry of a sheep.
BLEAT, v.i. [Sax. blaetan.] To make the noise of a sheep.
LOWING, n. The bellowing or cry of cattle.
OBEY, v.t. [L. obedio; ob and audio, to hear.] To comply with the commands, orders or instructions of a superior.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 15:14
And Samuel said, What meaneth then this bleating of the sheep in mine ears, and the lowing of the oxen which I hear?
1 Samuel 15:22
And Samuel said, Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.
1 Samuel 15:23
For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Because thou hast rejected the word of the LORD, he hath also rejected thee from being king.
Judges 5:16
Why abodest thou among the sheepfolds, to hear the bleatings of the flocks? For the divisions of Reuben there were great searchings of heart.
corruption_summary: Partial obedience is presented as obedience, and the part withheld is dedicated to God, so that the disobedience arrives wrapped in worship.
corruption_paragraphs: Saul's method is more sophisticated than plain refusal, and it is the method most available to religious people. He obeyed most of the command, kept back what he valued, and assigned the remainder to the LORD as sacrifice. Had Samuel not heard the sheep, the report would have stood. This is why 1 Samuel 15:22 is stated as a comparison rather than a prohibition — God does delight in sacrifice, He commanded it; He delights more in obedience, and an offering made out of what obedience required to be destroyed is not worship at all.

Verse 23 supplies the classification, and it is severe: rebellion is as witchcraft, stubbornness as idolatry. The reason is that all three are attempts to get an outcome on terms other than God's revealed word. The witch works around the word; the idolater substitutes for it; the stubborn man edits it. Judges 5:16 shows the quieter form of the same thing — Reuben sitting among the sheepfolds listening to the bleating, with great searchings of heart and no attendance at the battle. Deliberation is not obedience either.
roots_summary: Hebrew qol ha-tson (H6963 + H6629), the voice of the flock; shama (H8085), to hear, obey; meri (H4805), rebellion; qesem (H7081), divination, witchcraft.

Hebrew shama (H8085) — to hear and so to obey; the same root in both halves of verse 22.
Hebrew meri (H4805) — rebellion, bitterness; likened to witchcraft in verse 23.
Hebrew qesem (H7081) — divination; the comparison that ranks stubbornness with the occult.
Hebrew sheriqoth (H8292) — pipings, bleatings; Judges 5:16, what Reuben stayed to hear.
usage: “What meaneth then this bleating” — the evidence was simply audible.
“To obey is better than sacrifice” — a comparison, not a prohibition.
“Why abodest thou among the sheepfolds” — deliberation is not obedience.

pos: n. (a noxious field weed; the last word of Job's self-imprecation)
etymology: From Old English coccel, a weed growing among grain — probably the corn-cockle or darnel. Job 31:40 uses the Hebrew boshah, from a root meaning to stink, for whatever worthless growth a cursed field yields instead of barley.
biblical_def: Job ends his final defence by inviting a curse on his own land if he has lied about how he came by it: “If my land cry against me, or that the furrows likewise thereof complain” (Job 31:38) — then, he says, “Let thistles grow instead of wheat, and cockle instead of barley. The words of Job are ended” (Job 31:40). It is the most solemn form of oath available to a farmer, staking his livelihood on his innocence, and the narrator closes the speech with a line that reads like a gavel. The chapter he ends is a catalogue of the sins he has not committed, and several of them are sins no court could have tried: looking on a maid, rejoicing at an enemy's ruin, eating his morsel alone, trusting his gold. The weeds themselves belong to a curse older than Job's field — the ground cursed for Adam's sake, bringing forth thorns and thistles. Job invokes the fall as his surety. And the curse he calls down on a lying tongue lands elsewhere in the book on a barren field: “As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not; so he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end shall be a fool” (Jeremiah 17:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cockle as a weed that grows among corn, the cornrose or corn-campion — a plant of the genus Agrostemma.
webster_full: COCKLE, n. [Sax. coccel.] A plant, a weed that grows among corn, the cornrose, a species of Agrostemma.
COCKLE, n. A small testaceous shell-fish of the genus Cardium.
TARE, n. A weed that grows among corn; the darnel or lolium.

corruption_summary: Job's oath of innocence is read as self-righteousness, when Scripture allows a man to protest a false charge and God Himself vindicates the protest.
corruption_paragraphs: Job 31 makes modern readers uneasy, and it made his friends furious. A man lists sins he has not committed and stakes his fields on it. But the chapter is not a claim to sinlessness; it is a sworn denial of the specific accusations his comforters had brought — that his disasters proved secret crimes. Scripture permits and sometimes requires this. Paul answered the charges against him in detail; Samuel called Israel to testify whose ox he had taken. Refusing to defend a good name is not humility when the charge is false and the accusation is public.

The vindication comes from God Himself in chapter 42, where the friends — who had defended God's justice with a false account of Job's life — are told they have not spoken of Him the thing that is right. Job 31 is also a searching standard for any Christian who wants to use it as a mirror: it condemns looking on a maid, eating the morsel alone, rejoicing at an enemy's fall, and trusting in gold. Most defences of a reputation would not survive that chapter, which is precisely why Job could offer his fields.

pos: n. pl. (hard-shelled fruits; part of Jacob's present and the garden of the Song)
etymology: From Old English hnutu. Two different Hebrew words are rendered nuts: botnim in Genesis 43:11, pistachios, and egoz in the Song, the walnut — both prized and both grown in the land, not in Egypt.
biblical_def: Israel, forced to send Benjamin into Egypt, sends a present with him and chooses it carefully: “And their father Israel said unto them, If it must be so now, do this; take of the best fruits in the land in your vessels, and carry down the man a present, a little balm, and a little honey, spices, and myrrh, nuts, and almonds” (Genesis 43:11). Every item is a specialty of Canaan and none of them is a staple — there is a famine on, and a starving family is sending delicacies. The gift is an old man's courtesy under duress, and it is aimed, without his knowing it, at the son he thinks is dead. The other appearance is in the Song, where the beloved walks out to see whether anything is growing: “I went down into the garden of nuts to see the fruits of the valley, and to see whether the vine flourished, and the pomegranates budded” (Song of Solomon 6:11). Walnut groves, vines, and pomegranates belong to the vocabulary of a land at rest, the opposite of Genesis 43's famine. Scripture's catalogue of the good land is specific about its produce, and the specificity is part of the doctrine: the covenant God gives a real country with real trees in it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a nut as the fruit of certain trees and shrubs, consisting of a kernel covered by a hard shell.
webster_full: NUT, n. [Sax. hnut.] The fruit of certain trees and shrubs, consisting of a hard shell inclosing a kernel.
NUT, n. In mechanics, a small cylinder or other body, with teeth or wings; the small piece of metal with a screw cut in it, which is screwed on the end of a bolt.
ALMOND, n. [Fr. amande.] The fruit of the almond tree; a nut containing a kernel.
BALM, n. [L. balsamum.] The sap or juice of trees or shrubs remarkably odoriferous or aromatic.
PRESENT, n. That which is presented or given; a gift; a donative.

corruption_summary: Scripture's attention to ordinary produce is treated as incidental colour, and the goodness of created, edible, particular things is quietly spiritualized away.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The drift is a kind of piety that finds the material embarrassing. Genesis pauses in the middle of a famine narrative to name balm, honey, spices, myrrh, nuts, and almonds, and a reader trained to look only for doctrine skips the list. The principle to recover is that God made a world with pistachios in it and put the inventory in His book. Gnosticism has never stopped being the church's most persistent unacknowledged heresy, and it always begins by finding the physical beneath notice.

There is also a small pastoral lesson in Jacob's present. He is frightened, he has lost one son and is being made to risk another, and what he does is send a gift of the best his land can still produce. It changes nothing about the danger. It is the gesture of a man doing the one courteous thing left within his power while the outcome rests entirely elsewhere — and the reader, who knows who is waiting in Egypt, watches an old man's small kindness travel toward the son he is mourning.

pos: v. (to bring forth young from eggs; used of birds, of vipers, and of ill-gotten wealth)
etymology: From Middle English hacchen, to produce young from eggs. Scripture uses it three ways: of the owl in a desolate place, of the partridge that sits on eggs not hers, and of Isaiah's image for the plots of wicked men.
biblical_def: Jeremiah makes the failed hatching an image of dishonest wealth: “As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not; so he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end shall be a fool” (Jeremiah 17:11). The bird broods diligently over a clutch that will never come to anything, and the man who gathers by fraud is doing the same — real labour, real patience, and nothing at the end of it but the verdict fool. Isaiah uses the verb for the one creature that does successfully hatch in a land under judgment: “There shall the great owl make her nest, and lay, and hatch, and gather under her shadow: there shall the vultures also be gathered, every one with her mate” (Isaiah 34:15). Where a nation has been destroyed, the birds of the waste places breed undisturbed; the sign of desolation is not silence but the wrong things thriving. The prophets name the counterfeit source of guidance in the same register: “And when they shall say unto you, Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?” (Isaiah 8:19). And the covenant answer to a life of futile brooding is the ant's: “Provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest” (Proverbs 6:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hatch as to produce young from eggs by incubation; and figuratively, to contrive or plot; to form by meditation.
webster_full: HATCH, v.t. To produce young from eggs by incubation, or by artificial heat.
HATCH, v.t. To contrive or plot; to form by meditation, and bring to maturity; as, to hatch mischief.
HATCH, v.i. To produce young; to be disclosed from the egg.
INCUBATION, n. The act of sitting on eggs for the purpose of hatching young.
PARTRIDGE, n. [L. perdix.] A wild fowl of the genus Tetrao, an esteemed game bird.

corruption_summary: Wealth is judged by its amount and its legality rather than by whether it was got by right, which is the only question Jeremiah asks about it.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 17:11 does not say that riches are evil, and it does not say that riches are proof of blessing. It asks one question: was this got by right? That question is indifferent to scale and it survives every legal defence, because a great deal of what is got wrongly is got lawfully — a wage withheld on a technicality, a price extracted from someone with no alternative, a contract drafted to catch the unwary. The prosperity preacher and the class agitator both change the subject, one to the amount as evidence of favour, the other to the amount as evidence of guilt. Scripture asks about the getting.

The image is a mercy as well as a warning. The partridge is not lazy; she sits, and she sits patiently, and the eggs do not hatch. That is the true picture of a life built on gain wrongly obtained — not idleness but wasted diligence, and a man discovering in the midst of his days that the whole brood was empty. Verse 11 ends with the word fool, which in the Wisdom books is a moral and not an intellectual category. The clever man who arranged it all is the fool of the sentence.

pos: v.i. (to make broken, rapid sounds; Hezekiah's word for his own praying)
etymology: Imitative in origin, from the sound. Isaiah 38:14 uses the Hebrew tsaphaph, to chirp or twitter, of a sick king's prayer — the same verb Isaiah elsewhere uses, with contempt, of the muttering of mediums.
biblical_def: Hezekiah, told to set his house in order because he would die, wrote down afterward what his praying had sounded like: “Like a crane or a swallow, so did I chatter: I did mourn as a dove: mine eyes fail with looking upward: O LORD, I am oppressed; undertake for me” (Isaiah 38:14). It is not the language of a composed devotional life. A man in extremity makes bird-noises, and the last clause is four words long because that is all he could manage: undertake for me. The same register appears in Isaiah's picture of a people in distress: “We roar all like bears, and mourn sore like doves: we look for judgment, but there is none; for salvation, but it is far off from us” (Isaiah 59:11), and in the psalmist's isolation: “I watch, and am as a sparrow alone upon the house top” (Psalm 102:7). What makes the word remarkable is the company it keeps. Isaiah uses the same verb of the occult practitioners: “And when they shall say unto you, Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?” (Isaiah 8:19). The sound can be identical. Everything depends on who is being addressed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines chatter as to utter sounds rapidly and indistinctly, as a magpie or a monkey; to talk idly or carelessly; and of the teeth, to rattle.
webster_full: CHATTER, v.i. To utter sounds rapidly and indistinctly, as a magpie, or a monkey.
CHATTER, v.i. To talk idly, carelessly or rapidly; to jabber.
CHATTER, v.i. To make a noise by collision of the teeth, as in shivering.
MUTTER, v.i. To utter words with a low voice and compressed lips, with sullenness or in complaint; to grumble.
UNDERTAKE, v.t. To engage in; to enter upon; to become bound; to be surety for; to answer for.
scriptures: Isaiah 38:14
Like a crane or a swallow, so did I chatter: I did mourn as a dove: mine eyes fail with looking upward: O LORD, I am oppressed; undertake for me.
Isaiah 59:11
We roar all like bears, and mourn sore like doves: we look for judgment, but there is none; for salvation, but it is far off from us.
Psalm 102:7
I watch, and am as a sparrow alone upon the house top.
Isaiah 8:19
And when they shall say unto you, Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?
corruption_summary: Prayer is judged by its composure, so that a believer who can only chatter concludes he is not praying at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Hezekiah's record of his own prayer is one of the kindest things in Scripture for a person in genuine trouble. He does not report eloquence. He reports sounding like a swallow, mourning like a dove, and failing at the effort of looking up — and the prayer was heard, and fifteen years were added. A church culture that models prayer chiefly as articulate, ordered, and public will quietly teach its most afflicted members that what they are doing does not count. Romans 8 says the Spirit Himself makes intercession with groanings which cannot be uttered.

Isaiah 8:19 supplies the limit, and it is not about style. The wizards peep and mutter too; the sound is no different. What separates Hezekiah's chattering from the medium's muttering is the direction — should not a people seek unto their God? The occult is condemned in Scripture not because it is undignified but because it seeks the living to the dead. A groan aimed at the God who is there is prayer. An eloquence aimed anywhere else is not, whatever it sounds like.
